No, that's not right. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own, so your assistant won't remember what a student told it last week unless you build that in.

The mistake is an easy one to make. Inside a single chat it looks like the model remembers, because the app sends the whole conversation so far along with each new message. The model only ever sees what is in the text it is handed on that call. When a call ends, nothing is kept inside the model. Training also doesn't change this, because the model isn't learning from your students' chats.

Here is an example for your assistant. Last Tuesday, Sam says, "I finished the laser cutter safety training." Next Monday, Sam asks, "Can I book the laser cutter?" If your program sends only that new question, the model has no idea who Sam is or that the training happened. It may ask again or guess.

Memory is something your program builds, in three steps:
1. At the end of a session, the program saves a fact such as "Sam: laser cutter training done" to a file or database.
2. At the start of the next session, the program looks Sam up.
3. It puts that fact into the prompt, so the model reads it as part of its input.

That also ties to your budget. Everything you put back into the prompt costs tokens on every call, so you'll want to save short facts rather than whole transcripts.

Try this one: in your own words, who remembers Sam's training status between visits, the model or your program? What does the model see on Monday?

If you want, I can turn this into a short lesson on context and memory. That's the next step in your mission.
